mcqs.question: Why can't you compute a single, final "average order value" over an unbounded stream the way you would over a finite table?
options: Because the stream never ends, so the aggregate keeps changing forever unless you first bound it to a window of time
Because streams can only be aggregated using sliding windows
Because stream processors can't perform arithmetic on more than one event at a time
Because averages are undefined for any data arriving out of order
mcqs.explanation: Windowing exists precisely because an unbounded stream has no natural stopping point for an aggregate — you must define "over what period" for the number to mean anything. Streams can use any window type, not only sliding, and neither of the other two claims is true of stream processors generally.

mcqs.question: A dashboard reports "orders per 5-minute interval," with each interval's total final once computed and no interval sharing data with another. Which windowing style is this?
options: Sliding window
Tumbling window
Session window
Watermark-based window
mcqs.explanation: Fixed, non-overlapping, back-to-back buckets where each event belongs to exactly one interval is the definition of a tumbling window. Sliding windows overlap, session windows are gap-defined rather than fixed-width, and "watermark-based window" isn't a distinct window type.

mcqs.question: A metric recalculates "requests per second over the last 5 minutes" every 30 seconds, with each 5-minute window overlapping the previous one. Why can't you safely sum two of these windows to get a combined total?
options: Because sliding windows never share any events
Because the metric isn't computed correctly by the processor
Because the same event can fall inside multiple overlapping sliding windows, so summing would double-count it
Because sliding windows only work with session data
mcqs.explanation: Overlap is the whole point of a sliding window, and it's exactly why summing across windows double-counts shared events — the windows aren't additive by design. Nothing here implies a computation error, and sliding windows are unrelated to session data.

mcqs.question: A network delay causes a burst of events that happened around 10:00:00 to arrive at the stream processor around 10:00:45. If windowing is done by processing time, what happens?
options: Nothing — processing time and event time are always identical
The events are automatically re-timestamped to 10:00:00
The processor waits until the correct window opens before accepting them
The events land in the 10:00:45 window instead of the 10:00:00 window they actually belong to, corrupting both windows' counts
mcqs.explanation: Processing-time windowing groups events by when they arrive, so a delayed burst lands in whatever window is open at arrival time, inflating it while under-counting the window the events actually happened in. Processing time and event time diverge under load, and no automatic correction or wait-for-the-right-window behavior happens by default.

mcqs.question: What does a watermark let a stream processor do?
options: Declare an estimate of "no more events earlier than this event-time are expected" and use it to decide when to close a window
Guarantee that no event will ever arrive late
Convert processing time into event time automatically
Merge overlapping sliding windows into non-overlapping ones
mcqs.explanation: A watermark is an estimate, not a guarantee — it lets the processor decide a window is done enough to close and emit, while still allowing an "allowed lateness" grace period for stragglers. It doesn't eliminate late events, convert timestamps, or change how sliding windows overlap.
